newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish national airline Aer Lingus dispute worsens.
newsitem.headline: Irish national airline Aer Lingus dispute worsens.

text.p: Troubled Irish flag carrier Aer Lingus said on Tuesday that it was considering issuing protective notice of dismissal to all 6,000 employees if a strike warning by the company's 372 pilots was not withdrawn.
The dispute is coming to a head during one of the busiest months in Ireland's six-month EU presidency, and for which Aer Lingus had put on additional flights on its Brussels route.

The Irish Air Line Pilot's Association (IALPA) issued one week strike notice, effective from midnight on Sunday, in protest at the company's rejection of 17 per cent pay rise for pilots recommended by an independent tribunal.
"We have asked IALPA to respond to us by close of business today to the effect that they would withdraw their strike notice and enter into negotiations," a spokesman for Aer Lingus told Reuters.
"If they don't do that then we are going to have to consider putting people on protective notice."
Captain Dermot Rafferty, chairman of IALPA described the Aer Lingus protective notice threat as unworthy scare tactics".
Rafferty said IALPA was available for talks with Aer Lingus but only to discuss the implementation of the first phase of the 17 per cent pay rise, five per cent of which is due in October.
"If things do not change (before Sunday) the strike will take place on Sunday midnight," Rafferty added.

Aer Lingus, which has a total payroll of 136 million punts, said a 17 per cent pay rise on top of its existing payroll would effectively wipe out the total savings achieved under a restructuring plan known as the Cahill Plan.

The Aer Lingus spokesman said the company already faced demands for pay rises from other sections of the company who he said would use a concession of 17 per cent to pilots as a base marker for their pay demands.
The Cahill Plan came into effect in 1993 after the airline declared losses of 188 million punts ($302.4 million).
A special dispensation by the EU allowed the Irish government to inject 175 million punts over three years into Aer Lingus on condition that it implemented certain cost savings.
The plan also called for 1,530 job cuts, 12 percent of the workforce at the time and the disposal of assets such as its Copthorne hotel chain.

The group disposed of the 18-strong hotel chain to Singapore-based CDL Hotels International in August 1995 but has been dogged by disputes from various segments of the company over the last four years.
The company made a pre-tax profit of 17.8 million punts for the year to December 1995, its first profit for years.
